title: The New Moon Feast and the Arrows in the Field
summary: David, now certain that Saul means to kill him, asks Jonathan for help. Jonathan, still hoping it isn't so, agrees to test his father at the New Moon feast, and the two renew their covenant, with Jonathan asking David to keep faith with his household forever. When David's seat stays empty, Saul erupts, curses Jonathan, and hurls a spear at his own son. Jonathan signals the danger with arrows shot in the field, and the two friends part in tears.
story: Chapter 19 closed with Saul lying before Samuel at Ramah while David escaped. Chapter 20 is the last time David and Jonathan are together at Saul's court, and after it David never returns there. The chapter settles the question of whether reconciliation with Saul is possible; it is not. It also turns the friendship of chapter 18 into a covenant that reaches beyond both men's lifetimes. Jonathan openly acknowledges that the LORD will cut off David's enemies and asks David to protect his descendants when that day comes. David will keep that promise in 2 Samuel 9, when he brings Jonathan's son Mephibosheth to his own table.
historical:
The setting is Saul's court at Gibeah and the fields nearby. The seating in verse 25 gives a glimpse of the court: the king by the wall, with Jonathan opposite and Abner, the army commander and Saul's cousin, beside him, and a place kept for David as the king's son-in-law and commander. It is a small circle, which is why an empty seat was noticed at once.

The annual clan sacrifice at Bethlehem mentioned in David's cover story (verses 6 and 29) reflects the importance of extended families in Israel's life. Clans held their own sacrificial meals, often at local places of worship, before the temple in Jerusalem became the one central sanctuary. Whether David's excuse was true or invented, it was believable enough that Saul would have accepted it had he not already intended harm.
cultural:
The New Moon, the first day of each month in Israel's lunar calendar, was a sacred day marked by special offerings and the blowing of trumpets (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15). At Saul's court it involved a feast lasting at least two days. Because the meal was connected with sacrifice, a person who was ritually unclean (through contact with a corpse, for example, or a bodily discharge) could not take part, which is why Saul first assumes David is unclean (verse 26). Ritual uncleanness was not the same as sin; it was a temporary state that barred a person from holy things until washing and waiting restored them.

Saul's insult to Jonathan in verse 30 attacks his mother in order to shame the son, a way of saying Jonathan is disloyal by nature. Saul also states the political reality plainly: as long as David lives, Jonathan will not be king. In the ancient world, a new dynasty commonly wiped out the family of the old one, which is why Jonathan's request that David never cut off his kindness from his household (verses 14 and 15) was far from a formality. The arrow signal gave Jonathan a way to warn David without being seen talking to him, since an archer's servant retrieving arrows was an ordinary sight.
literary: The chapter is one of the longest dialogues in Samuel, and it moves between two scenes: the field, where David and Jonathan speak privately, and the table, where Saul's intentions are revealed. It is built around a plan and its execution. The plan is laid out in detail (verses 18 to 23), the test takes place over two days (verses 24 to 34), and the signal is carried out exactly as arranged (verses 35 to 40). Key words recur: the LORD as witness, loving devotion (hesed), and the covenant between the two houses. The chapter frames the whole episode with oaths by the LORD, one at the start (verse 3) and one at the end (verse 42), so that the friendship is set within God's presence. The final scene is spare and moving, and the narrator's small note that “David wept more” says a great deal with a few words.

outline.t: The covenant between Jonathan and the house of David
The plan: the New Moon and the arrows
The empty seat and Saul's rage against Jonathan
The arrows in the field and the parting of friends

doctrines.note: Jonathan's covenant with David binds their families across generations and is made “before the LORD,” with the LORD as witness. It shows covenant as a relationship of sworn loyalty that outlasts changing circumstances.

Jonathan recognizes that the LORD will establish David and cut off his enemies, even though this means Jonathan himself will not be king. He submits to God's purpose rather than fighting it, where Saul resists the same purpose with a spear.

The chapter shows a family torn by a father's jealousy. Jonathan has to choose between loyalty to his father and loyalty to what is right, and he chooses rightly at great personal cost, while still honoring his father as far as he can.

words.note: Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love, or covenant kindness. It is loyalty that goes beyond obligation, the faithfulness that keeps a promise when it would be easier to let it go. Jonathan asks for “the LORD's loving devotion,” asking David to treat his family the way God treats his people.
Berit, covenant. David appeals to it in verse 8 (“you have brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD”). The covenant is sworn by God's name, which makes God its witness and guarantor.

Chodesh, month or new moon. Israel's months began with the new moon, marked as a holy day. The same word gives the chapter its timetable and explains why David's absence from the royal table would be noticed.

Shalom, peace, well-being, or safety. In verse 7 it means that David would be safe; in verse 42 Jonathan sends him away “in peace.” The word means wholeness and security, not merely the absence of conflict, and here it is spoken in the middle of danger.

christ: Jonathan's plea that David show him “the LORD's loving devotion” introduces a theme that runs through David's story and beyond it: the steadfast love that the LORD promises David's house (2 Samuel 7:15; Isaiah 55:3). Paul quotes the Greek form of Isaiah 55:3 in Acts 13:34 when he speaks of Christ's resurrection as the fulfillment of the holy and sure blessings promised to David. In a thematic rather than predictive way, Jonathan also models the response the New Testament asks of every reader toward the true son of David: to recognize God's chosen king, to yield one's own claims to him, and to trust his covenant faithfulness for oneself and one's family.

hard.q: Why did David propose lying to Saul about going to Bethlehem, and does the Bible approve of it?
hard.a: David's plan relies on a cover story, and the text does not say whether he actually went to Bethlehem. Readers respond in different ways. Some argue that the excuse may have been true, or that it was a legitimate means of testing a king who had already tried to murder David and had broken a sworn oath (19:6). Others hold that it was a real deception and that the Bible, as often, simply reports it without approval, allowing readers to see that David's faith was genuine but not flawless; he will use deception again in chapter 21 with serious consequences. The chapter's focus is elsewhere: on the covenant between the two friends and the revelation of Saul's intent. It neither holds up David's cover story as a model nor condemns it outright.

questions: Jonathan asked David to keep faith with his family long after Jonathan was gone. What commitments are you making now that will matter to people who come after you?
Jonathan chose what was right over his father's favor and his own prospects. When has loyalty to God put you at odds with someone you love?
The friends parted not knowing if they would meet again. What does their friendship teach about the kind of friends worth having and being?
